amendments.rule: Gapping is not a new case. When a parallel line omits its verb, the copula the ASV supplies joins the predicate that licenses it, exactly as in rule 20, and is never `added`. **But that covers the copula and nothing more, exactly as rule 20's own boundary does.** Where the line's missing verb is a lexical one and the ASV writes a lexical verb for it, no morpheme in that line is there to carry the word, and it is its own `added` unit under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause: `כִּי־מַפְרִיס פַּרְסָה הוּא וְלֹא גֵרָה` → *because he parteth the hoof but* ***cheweth*** *not the cud* gives *but* to the waw under rule 14, *not* to the negative, and *the cud* to the noun with its supplied *the* under rule 15, leaving the supplied *cheweth* `added`. Do not read *omits its verb* above as a licence to fold such a word into the negative, the connective or the noun standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do — drop the English verb and ask whether a morpheme standing in that line has lost its rendering, or whether what has gone is a predication the Hebrew never wrote there. **But read whether the Hebrew writes that verb anywhere in the coordination before counting.** Where a verb the Hebrew writes once is realized twice across coordinated clauses, both occurrences are that verb's one possibly discontinuous unit under rule 25, exactly as a distributed `מִן` takes both of its *from*s there; what the preceding sentences govern is a line whose verb the Hebrew leaves unwritten altogether. **And the second realization need not repeat the first's English words.** English answers a gapped verb with a pro-verb as readily as with a repetition, so where the ASV writes *doth*, *do* or *did* for the colon whose verb the Hebrew gaps, or rewrites that verb's clause in other words, the word realizes the verb the Hebrew wrote once and joins its one discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first occurrence's lexical verb: `שֶׁמֶן וּקְטֹרֶת יְשַׂמַּח־לֵב וּמֶתֶק רֵעֵהוּ` → *Oil and perfume* ***rejoice*** *the heart, So* ***doth*** *the sweetness of a man's friend* gives both *rejoice* and *doth* to the one `יְשַׂמַּח`, while the waw keeps the *So* rule 14 writes for it. What tells such a word from the supplied lexical verb of the preceding sentences is whether the Hebrew writes the verb it stands for anywhere in the coordination, and not whether the ASV wrote the same English twice: a pro-verb names the very verb the first colon writes, while *cheweth* above names an action the Hebrew never wrote in that verse at all. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it either way and decides nothing, by rule 7.
amendments.why: PRO.27.9 writes *Oil and perfume rejoice the heart: So doth the sweetness of a man's friend*, where the second colon gaps יְשַׂמַּח and the ASV answers it with the pro-verb *doth*. Rule 34's closing paragraph already gives a verb written once and realized twice to that verb, but its example and its analogy to a distributed מִן are both repetitions of the same English word, so a later pass could read *doth* as the supplied lexical verb the rule's own first half marks `added`. The amendment states the boundary the rule already implies — the pro-verb names the written verb, *cheweth* names an action the Hebrew never wrote — and keeps the test on what the Hebrew writes rather than on what English words the ASV repeated. PRO.27.13, where the ASV instead repeats the whole clause *that is surety for* over the coordinated member, is the same ruling with identical words and shows the two shapes belong together.

conventions: PRO.27 italics: this chapter's ASV marks eight supplied words, and each was counted against the morphemes of its own clause rather than accepted or rejected as a class (rule 7). Where no morpheme answers, the word is `added`: the three italic connectives of 27.12 and the italic *And* of 27.23, none of which has a waw in its clause, and the italic *answereth* of 27.19 and *tried* of 27.21, whose Hebrew lines write no verb. Where a morpheme answers, the italic joins it: the *doth* of 27.9 and the repeated *that is surety for* of 27.13 are second realizations of a verb the Hebrew writes once, and the *there will be* of 27.27 is the construction's copula and dummy on the לְ heading the predicate.

PRO.27 draws the rule 20 boundary between a linking verb and a supplied lexical verb twice, in the same construction and opposite ways. At 27.24 *endure* in *doth the crown endure unto all generations* joins the לְ under rules 20 and 49, because it links the subject to a prepositional predicate the Hebrew writes and adds no participant. At 27.21 *is tried* in *a man is tried by his praise* is `added` whole, auxiliary included, because it introduces an event and an agent the Hebrew never wrote and the לְפִי beside it has already spent its word on *by*.

PRO.27 renders four construct chains attributively rather than with *of* (rule 28): גֹּאֶה-type pairs at 27.9 (*hearty counsel*), 27.15 (*a very rainy day*, *a contentious woman*) and 27.27 (*goats milk*). In each the rectum keeps only its attributive word and no relational word is placed, while the chains rendered with *of* at 27.9, 27.10, 27.17, 27.19, 27.20, 27.23, 27.25, 27.26 and 27.27 put that word on the rectum. The chapter reads which shape the ASV wrote rather than the Hebrew's construct state.

PRO.27 marks one unit `noncompositional` — שִׁית לֵב → *look well* at 27.23, where neither English word writes either morpheme's lexeme, so rule 6's fallback anchors the source head on the first token. The chapter's four preposition-plus-construct fusions (27.1, 27.4, 27.21, 27.22) are `aligned`, following rule 30 rather than rule 6. The corpus records both statuses for such fusions, so the split here is a chapter convention and not a finding about either verse.

report: Read all 27 verses end to end as well as the 33-lemma candidate table, since the table is keyed by source lemma and this chapter carries eight `added` units that appear in no group. No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference, so patches is empty.

Preposition-plus-construct fusion was the closest call. בְּיוֹם fuses to a single *of* at PRO.27.1 and splits into *in* (בְּ) and *a day* (יוֹם) at PRO.27.15. That is rule 30's one-rendering condition read by subtraction, not a split: at 27.1 the ASV writes no word for יוֹם at all, at 27.15 it writes one for each morpheme. The chapter's other fusions — לִפְנֵי → *before* (27.4), לְפִי → *by* (27.21), בְּתוֹךְ → *along with* (27.22) — all head on the construct noun, while מֵעַל → *from* (27.22) heads on מִן under rule 23's second clause, which is the two-preposition case and not the preposition-plus-construct one.

Rule 31 heads on single Hebrew nouns rendered by modifier plus noun look inconsistent and are not. יָמִין → *right hand* and תְּאֵנָה → *the fig tree* head on the modifier, because the English noun alone is any hand, any tree. רִיפוֹת → *bruised grain* and דֶּשֶׁא → *the tender grass* head on the noun, because *grain* and *grass* are class nouns the ASV writes alone for words of that class — 27.25's own margin glosses חָצִיר as *grass*. One test, four lexemes, four answers.

Supplied English is counted the same way throughout: `added` where no morpheme in the clause answers to it (27.12's three italic connectives and 27.23's italic *And*, no waw standing in either clause; 27.19 *answereth* and 27.21 *is tried*, clauses whose Hebrew writes no verb), and kept with the morpheme that does answer (27.9 *doth* and 27.13's repeated *that is surety for*, both second realizations of a written verb; 27.27's *there will be* on the לְ heading the predicate). The one boundary judgment is 27.24's *endure*, read as rule 20's linking verb on the לְ rather than as a supplied lexical verb, and it is recorded as a convention.

Verbless-clause copula placement is uniform: prepositional predicate takes it on the preposition (27.21, 27.24, 27.26 line 1, 27.27), nominal or adjectival predicate takes it on the predicate word (27.3, 27.5, 27.6, 27.7, 27.8, 27.10, 27.26 line 2). 27.21's *is tried* is not a counter-example — rule 20's own boundary says a preposition on which the ASV has already spent a word (here *by* for לְפִי) carries nothing further, so the whole passive phrase is the supplied lexical verb.

Articles: every written or assimilated הַ takes a *the* the ASV wrote before its own word (27.14, 27.19 s011, 27.20 s008) and is `unrepresented` where none is written (27.19, 27.21 twice, 27.22 twice). The two rectum articles at 27.19 and 27.20 are both fronted under rule 29 in the same construction; the supplied *the*s at 27.25, 27.26 and 27.27 all sit on nouns carrying no article morpheme. Nothing to reconcile.

BSB: all six disagreements are documented convention differences, none an error. Three (27.19 [הַ], 27.22 הָ twice) are articles the ASV writes no *the* for; 27.17 בְּ is silenced by *Iron sharpeneth iron*, which promotes its object to a direct object under rule 40; 27.11 דָבָר is left unrendered by *answer him that reproacheth me*; 27.24's second דּוֹר is the unrendered occurrence of a repetition the ASV writes once as *all generations*, and either occurrence being the rendered one leaves BSB disagreeing. No accepted edge was changed.
